newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman says US no-fly coalition has GCC support.
newsitem.headline: Oman says US no-fly coalition has GCC support.

text.p: An Omani minister said on Saturday that Gulf Arab states supported the United States" declaration, backed by Britain, extending a no-fly zone in southern Iraq to its 33rd parallel.

He spoke after Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers held two rounds of talks in Saudi Arabia which included how to forge a response to missile strikes against Iraq by the U.S., their key Western ally.
Much of the Arab world has condemned the attacks as infringing on Iraq's sovereignty.
Diplomats say there were signs of differing opinions in the GCC, which Iraq has asked for support.
On extending the no-fly zone, policed by allied warplanes, Oman's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Youssef bin Alawi bin Abdullah told reporters late on Saturday:
"The GCC is with the U.S.-led international coalition...we support the coalition in this regard."

Abdullah said the GCC's Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and United Arab Emirates formed a committee to draw up a position on Iraq. They are due to hold further talks on Sunday and issue an official statement.
The six states are key allies of the United States, whose planes fly from the Gulf to patrol southern Iraq as part of a coalition to enforce the post-Gulf War no-fly zones.

Washington decided on Tuesday to extend the zone from the 32nd parallel where it was fixed after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War. The U.S. says the wider zone is aimed at further restricting Iraq's ability to pose a threat to its neighbours.
The U.S. used its warships deployed in the Gulf to launch missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday against Iraqi defence targets. Iraq said some citizens were killed in the attacks.
The United States said the missile strikes were in response to the Iraqi army's intervention in northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction seize a city from a rival group a week ago.
The official Qatar news agency on Saturday reported that Qatar's Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jabr al-Thani said Iraq had a right to protect its territory.

"On the recent developments in northern Iraq...(he) said these events should come to an end," according to the Arabic text of Sheikh Hamad's comments to CNN. He also said the U.S. should work for "another approach" to the problem.
The GCC said the ministers' meeting, planned before the strikes, was significant and would include terrorism, ties with Iran and Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
